_about: Longer 'what is in this area' text and the group descriptions shown on the dictionary page. Keyed by domain id (see domains.json). Optional: a domain without a summary shows its short description from the registry. Group names must match the 'group' field of the entries.

economy.visitor-economy.summary: This area holds the Data Observatory's data on tourism places in Puerto Rico: counts for each of the 78 municipalities, the list of individual places, and the rules used to sort and count them. It helps you see where attractions, food and drink places, lodging and visitor services are, and what mix each municipality has; compare per resident or per square kilometre, because raw counts mostly show which municipalities are big. Keep two limits in mind: each place is a listing from Overture Maps, an open map-data project, so it is not a business, a room, a visitor or a job; and the data are a snapshot from one Overture release, so they show no growth or decline.

groups.Tourism places counted: Municipality totals of tourism places: the main count, two larger counts that use looser rules, counts by category, places with a website, and the average Overture confidence score.
groups.Tourism places relative to people and la: Each municipality's tourism places per 1,000 residents (2020 Census) and per square kilometre of land, which let you compare municipalities of different sizes.
groups.Tourism places: categories: One entry for each of the four tourism categories (Attractions, Gastronomy meaning food and drink, Accommodations and Visitor services), saying which types it holds and how places reach it.
groups.Tourism places: classification: The three fields that sort each place: its tourism category, its more specific type, and the original Overture category it came from.
groups.Tourism places: how the data are made: Method notes on how the places list is made: how Overture categories are sorted, which places are counted, how duplicates are merged, how each place gets a municipality and barrio and its flood, protected-area, land-use and transit fields, which Overture fields are left out, how to read a missing value, and the steps of the build.
groups.Tourism places: identity and location: The fields that say which place a listing is and where its pin sits: Overture ID, name, latitude and longitude, address text, website, municipality and barrio.
groups.Tourism places: quality and source: Fields about where a listing came from and how sure Overture is: its confidence score, the contributing source, the date the source updated its record (a data-version date, not a visit to the place), and how many duplicate listings were folded into the place.
groups.Tourism places: types: One entry for each place type found in the data, such as Beaches, Restaurants, Hotels or Marinas, showing which Overture categories it groups and how to read it.
groups.Tourism supply layers on the Analysis ta: The five Analysis tab layers that map tourism places by municipality (all places, lodging, restaurants and bars, attractions and visitor services), plus a note on how the tab builds them.
groups.Flood exposure by municipality: For each municipality, the number of counted tourism places in the 1% flood area, the number in the 1% or 0.2% areas together, and the share of its places in the 1% area.
groups.Flood exposure of tourism places: For each tourism place, the FEMA flood zone, zone subtype and high-risk (1%) flag at its map point, which are left out when the point is not in a mapped flood area.
groups.Protected-area exposure by municipality: For each municipality, the number of counted tourism places whose map point lies inside a protected area listed in PAD-US.
groups.Protected-area exposure of tourism place: For each tourism place, the name and protection level of the protected area that contains its map point, with the strictest level kept when the point lies in several areas.
groups.Barrios: tourism-place counts: For each barrio, counts of listed tourism places, places per square kilometer, places in a mapped flood hazard area, places within 400 meters of transit, and lodging places.
groups.Land use plan: place listings: How many place listings, and what share, sit on specially protected rural land or on urban land in each municipality, and the plan class and group at each place's map pin.
groups.Transit access of tourism places: How close tourism places are to transport: the distance and name of the nearest mapped stop of any kind, the distance to the nearest stop with a current timetable with its weekday departures and weekend service, and, for each municipality and barrio, the counts and shares of places near such stops, including those near only an expired or unscheduled stop.
groups.How places and points are built: How tourism places, transit stops and census blocks are assigned to a municipality, which places each municipal count includes, and how flood and protected-area exposure is counted for each municipality.
groups.Which places a percentage counts: Which set of places each municipal percentage is based on, tourism places for the transit shares and all place listings for the land-use plan shares, and why the two sets should not be compared directly.

population.summary: This area covers who lives in Puerto Rico and its 78 municipalities (how many people, how old they are and how many households there are) and helps show whether a place is gaining or losing residents or getting older. The numbers come from three Census Bureau sources (census counts, yearly estimates and five-year survey estimates) that cover different dates, so cite the source and period with each one. The yearly estimates switch to a new starting point in 2020, so do not read 2019 to 2020 as one year of change. The five-year survey estimates are also published for 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups, always with their margins of error: below the municipio they are rough, so read the margin every time.

groups.Change since 2008-2012: The percent change in each municipality's survey-based population estimate from the 2008-2012 period to the latest five-year survey period, which is not the same as the change between census counts.
groups.Disability and veterans: The share of civilian adults who are veterans and the share of people living outside institutions who have a disability, from survey estimates with margins of error, for municipios, barrios and census tracts.
groups.Household types: The share of households that are family households and the share that are one person living alone, from survey estimates with margins of error, for municipios, barrios and census tracts.
groups.Households: How many households (homes where people live) there are and how many people live in each one on average, from five-year survey estimates that carry a margin of error.
groups.People and age: How many people the survey counts in each area and what share are women, under 18 or 65 and older, for municipios, barrios, census tracts and block groups, with margins of error.
groups.People counted in the census: The 2010 and 2020 census counts of residents for each municipality, and the percent change between the two counts.
groups.Population: How many people live in each municipality and in Puerto Rico each year since 2010, how much that number has changed since the 2010 and 2020 censuses, and how old residents are (the share aged 65 and over, and the median age, which is the age that splits residents in half).
groups.Residents exposed to hazards, protected: How many residents live inside a FEMA flood hazard area, in the area flooded by 1 to 10 feet of sea level rise, inside a protected area, or within 400 m of a transit stop, for each municipio, barrio and census tract, counted from 2020 Census blocks.
groups.Language: The share of people 5 and older who say they speak English less than "very well", from survey estimates with margins of error, for municipios, barrios and census tracts.
groups.Daytime population: How many people are in each municipio on a working day, how much commuting adds to or takes from its residents, and the share of its workers who work in another municipio: calculated from the Census Bureau's commuting flows of 2016-2020 and the 2020 Census, with margins of error.
groups.Net migration by age: How many people each municipio gained or lost to migration between the 2010 and 2020 censuses, by age group (estimates by the residual method).

housing.summary: This area describes the homes of Puerto Rico and its 78 municipalities: how many there are, how many are empty, who lives in them, what they cost, and how much income households spend on rent or owner costs. It also reproduces tables from the Foundation for Puerto Rico 2023 study The State of Housing in Puerto Rico, so you can compare places and years, for example where many homes sit empty or are kept for occasional use, how rents and home values changed, and how many households spend a large share of income on housing. Keep two things in mind: most figures are survey estimates that pool five years of answers and carry a margin of error, so small municipalities can swing widely; and an empty home is not an abandoned home, because the counts include homes for rent, for sale and for weekend use.

groups.Affordability: A yardstick that compares the typical home value with the largest 30-year loan a household with the typical income could carry under fixed assumptions (30% of income for housing and a 5% interest rate), which is not what a bank would lend.
groups.Change since 2008-2012: How much each municipality's median home value and median rent changed, in percent, between the 2008-2012 survey period and the latest one, without any adjustment for inflation.
groups.Cost burden: How much household income goes to housing: the typical share of income renters spend on rent, and the share of renters, and of owners with a mortgage, who spend 30% or more of income on housing (for renters also 50% or more), with households that have no cash rent or no income left out.
groups.Homes counted in the census: The number of homes the census counted in each municipality on April 1, 2010 and April 1, 2020, whether or not anyone lived in them.
groups.Housing stock: How many homes there are and what they are like: counts and shares of homes, empty homes and the reasons they are empty (for rent, for sale, seasonal or other), building types, age of homes, crowding, and residents per home, from the 10-year census and the Census Bureau's five-year survey.
groups.Owners and renters: The share of occupied homes that are lived in by their owners, with the rest rented.
groups.Prices and costs: Typical (median) home values as owners estimate them, typical monthly rents, and typical monthly costs of owning a home with and without a mortgage, in the dollars of each survey period.
groups.State of Housing study (2023): Tables and figures printed in the Foundation for Puerto Rico 2023 study (population change, rent and owner-cost bands, ownership by age, tax credit housing projects, headline numbers and the municipality profile), with live versions recalculated from Census Bureau data for some tables.
groups.Survey window: The last year of the five-year Census Bureau survey period behind the municipality housing figures, where a value of 2024 means the years 2020 to 2024.
groups.Housing methods: How the observatory calculates the housing affordability figures (the largest loan a household with the median income could carry, compared with the median home value) and the changes since the 2008-2012 survey window.
groups.Homes exposed to hazards, protected land: How many housing units sit inside a FEMA flood hazard area, in the area flooded by 1 to 10 feet of sea level rise, inside a protected area, or within 400 m of a transit stop, for each municipio, barrio and census tract, counted from 2020 Census blocks.
groups.Home loans: Home loans made and denied in each municipio every year since 2018, from the lenders' reports under the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA): counts and sums only.

economy.summary: This area holds figures on jobs, industries, unemployment, income, poverty, education, commuting, and household vehicles and internet access, for the 78 municipalities and, for most figures, for Puerto Rico as a whole. It helps answer where the jobs are, who is looking for work and how much households earn, but jobs and wages are counted where the employer is, while workers and household income are counted where people live, so the two can differ. Survey and unemployment figures are estimates that are less precise for small municipalities, and a blank industry job count means the figure was withheld or not published, not zero.

groups.Change since 2008-2012: How much median household income and the share of adults with a bachelor's degree changed in each municipality between the 2008-2012 survey period and the latest one; the income change is in dollars not adjusted for price rises.
groups.Income and poverty: How much households earn and how many people live below the poverty level, from five-year Census Bureau surveys: median and per capita income, median income of owner and renter households, shares of households under $25,000 and at $75,000 or more, an income inequality score (the Gini index), and the poverty rate.
groups.Industries: Yearly private-sector job counts for each of the 19 industry sectors, jobs in tourism-related industries (hotels, restaurants, arts and recreation), a score of how concentrated local jobs are in a few industries, and the industry or government group with the most jobs.
groups.Jobs and employers: Yearly counts of all, private-sector and government jobs, work sites and pay at employers located in each municipality, from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, plus the government share of jobs and the number of jobs for each employed resident.
groups.Labor force: Estimates of residents who work or are looking for work, counted where they live: yearly US Bureau of Labor Statistics figures (labor force, employed, unemployed and the unemployment rate), five-year Census Bureau survey rates (employment and unemployment), and a note on how the Bureau figures are built; the two sources are not comparable.
groups.Labor force by sex: Labor force participation and unemployment of women and men, from the Census Bureau's five-year survey (table B23001) in three windows that share no year (2010-2014, 2015-2019, 2020-2024), with 90% margins of error: the participation rates of women 16 and over, men 16 and over and women 25 to 54, the gap between men and women, the unemployment rate of women, and the counts of women behind them; also the file of the Women in the labor force page, which holds the counts by sex and age for every municipio and region.
groups.Workers and commuting: Employed residents, counted where they live, by whether they work for government, a nonprofit or themselves, and by how they usually get to work (driving alone, public transportation, walking, working from home) and how long the trip takes, from five-year Census Bureau surveys.
groups.Jobs and money: How the jobs, work-site and wage figures are counted, why some job figures are withheld and left blank, and which figures count where work is done, where people live or another place.
groups.Global Innovation Index: FPR's 2021 Global Innovation Index profile of Puerto Rico (GII 2020 method), frozen as printed, with the newest open value of each indicator that can be updated and an indicative position among the GII 2026 economies where the sources match (gii_profile.json, the Global Innovation Index page of the Knowledge Area).
groups.Prices and inflation: Consumer prices in Puerto Rico (the Department of Labor and Human Resources' index) and in the United States (the Bureau of Labor Statistics' CPI-U) by month since 2000: 12-month inflation, yearly averages, the 8 major groups, a five-year projection from expected US inflation with error bands tested on the past, median household income in constant dollars and Social Security's cost-of-living adjustments.
groups.Poverty and assistance: The share of households that received nutrition assistance (PAN), for municipios, barrios and census tracts, and the share of children under 18 and of people 65 and older below the poverty level, for municipios; survey estimates with margins of error.
groups.Banks and deposits: The offices of FDIC-insured banks in each municipio and the deposits booked at them, every June 30 since 2000 (FDIC Summary of Deposits). Cooperativas are not in it.
groups.Jobs within reach: How many jobs residents can reach within 30 and 45 minutes by car, and what share of Puerto Rico's jobs that is, by municipio (estimates).

public-money.summary: This area shows federal contracts, grants, direct payments, loans and other aid recorded for each of Puerto Rico's 78 municipalities and for the island as a whole, by federal fiscal year, and disaster aid that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) approved after the disasters declared each year. It helps you see where federal money is recorded, how that changes over time, and how much disaster aid was approved for public bodies and for households. Keep two limits in mind: the dollar figures are money promised or approved, not money spent, and none of the figures measures damage or need; and a municipality's figure counts only the money an agency recorded to that place, so San Juan's federal award figures can include money meant for the whole island, and some federal award and FEMA Public Assistance money names no municipality at all.

groups.Disaster recovery: Disaster aid from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), by municipality and by the year a disaster was declared: Public Assistance dollars for public bodies, the share of those dollars that FEMA records as statewide with no municipality named, and the households and dollars approved for individual help.
groups.Federal awards by place of performance: Money the federal government committed to Puerto Rico, as one total and five types (contracts, grants, direct payments, loans counted at their estimated cost, and other aid), for each municipality and the whole island by federal fiscal year, with an explanation of how awards are assigned to a place.

hazards.summary: This area holds US federal data on flood zones, sea level rise, past storms and protected land in Puerto Rico, plus the flags and counts that show which tourism places, and how many in each municipality, fall inside flood zones and protected areas. It helps you ask which places sit in a mapped flood area, which storms came near the island and how strong their winds were, what a set height of sea level rise could cover, and which places lie on land listed as protected. Two limits matter most: these layers describe hazard, not damage, flood depth in a given storm or insurance, and the place flags test only one map point per place; and "protected" means listed in a protected-areas database that includes local parks and military land, not only nature reserves.

groups.Flood hazard zones (FEMA): The flood zone map of the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) for Puerto Rico: the zone code, subtype and high-risk flag on each map shape, how the map layer draws them, how a place is flagged, and what the zones cannot tell you.
groups.Hurricanes and tropical storms: Atlantic storms from NOAA's Hurricane Database that came within 250 km (about 155 miles) of the centre of Puerto Rico: how they are chosen, each storm's name, year, winds, category, closest distance and track, the hurricane scale, the 3D map layer, and the limits of the data.
groups.Sea level rise: The sea level rise map layers from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), which the observatory shows live without storing them, and the rule that turns a year and a scenario in the 3D view into a whole number of feet.
groups.Social Vulnerability Index (CDC/ATSDR): CDC's Social Vulnerability Index 2022 for each municipio: the overall rank and the ranks for socioeconomic status, household characteristics, and housing type and transportation, each from 0 (least vulnerable) to 1 (most), among the 78 municipios of Puerto Rico only.
groups.Facilities and roads in hazard zones: How many public facilities, public school students and kilometres of main road in each municipio stand inside three hazard areas: FEMA's 1% annual chance flood area, NOAA's 3 ft sea level rise area and the USGS map's high landslide susceptibility classes. The observatory's layers laid on the hazard maps: it says where they stand, not that harm will come to them.
groups.Drought: How much of each municipio was in drought, every year since 2000, from the weekly US Drought Monitor: the average share of the area and the weeks with drought over half of it.
groups.Storm recovery: How long night-time light took to come back after Hurricanes María (2017) and Fiona (2022), and how dark each area got, by barrio and municipio.
groups.Cut off from hospitals: How many residents would have no open road to a hospital when the roads in FEMA's flood area or the bridges in poor condition close, by barrio and municipio (estimates, a worst case).

environment.land.summary: This area holds the outlines and land areas of Puerto Rico's 78 municipalities and 901 barrios (districts inside municipalities), and the 2015 land-use plan of the Planning Board (Junta de Planificación), summed by municipality and matched to place listings. It helps you see where a municipality or barrio starts and ends, how much land it covers, and how the plan classes that land. Keep two limits in mind: the outlines are simplified Census Bureau shapes cut at the shoreline, so they suit maps but not checking a single lot, and the plan is a 2015 planning label, not zoning and not a record of what stands on the land today.

groups.Protected areas (PAD-US): The records of the US Geological Survey's Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US) for Puerto Rico: each area's name, type, protection level, public access, manager and size, the map layer, and how a place is flagged as inside one.
groups.Land use plan: area: For each municipality, the land area in each plan group and the share of its classified land that is urban, urbanizable, ordinary rural or specially protected rural.
groups.Land use plan: classes and methods: A guide to the plan's class codes and the six groups made from them, and the steps used to compute land shares and place shares.
groups.Land-use plan: classes: One entry for each of the plan's 17 class codes, such as urban land, ordinary rural land, the types of protected rural land, water and roads.
groups.Land-use plan: groups: One entry for each of the six broad groups this site sorts the plan's classes into: urban, urbanizable, ordinary rural, protected rural, water and road.
groups.Land-use plan: map layer and fields: The 2015 land-use plan as a map layer, and the fields in it: class code, class name, group, display color and the municipality the plan names.
groups.Land-use plan: methods: How land-use shares are computed from the plan's own area figures, and how each place listing gets its plan class from its map pin.
groups.Zoning (Calificación): One entry on the Planning Board's zoning districts (Calificación), which this site does not publish, and why the plan's land classes must not be read as zoning.

infrastructure.mobility.summary: This area describes public transit, airports and the road network: where stops, stations, terminals and route lines are, which operators publish timetables, how many residents and tourism places are near a stop, and where people live far from service. It helps answer who has a scheduled stop nearby and where different systems could connect. Keep two limits in mind: "near a stop" means within 400 m in a straight line of a stop in a published timetable, which says nothing about how often vehicles run or whether people can walk there; and the data hold timetables and volunteer-mapped points, not live vehicle positions, so services with no published timetable, such as públicos (shared cars and vans that run set routes), are missing from the resident coverage figures.

groups.Vehicles and internet: The share of households with no vehicle, with an internet subscription and with no internet access, from five-year Census Bureau surveys.
groups.Airports, taxis and charging: Airports and airfields from the Federal Aviation Administration list and OpenStreetMap, plus taxi stands and electric vehicle charging points that volunteers mapped, as counts for each municipality and as point details such as airport codes and public use; volunteer mapping is uneven, so a zero for taxi stands or charging points does not mean there are none.
groups.Municipal transit systems: Whether a municipality runs its own bus or trolley system that reports to the federal transit database, whether that system's public timetable is still valid, and how many routes it lists.
groups.Operators and timetable feeds: The transit operators the observatory lists, how that list is made, and whether each operator's published timetable (its feed) is current, about to expire, expired or missing, with the feed's dates and flags.
groups.Real-time data: Which public sources of live vehicle positions were checked, what each one needs, and the date of the check; the observatory holds no live vehicle positions.
groups.Ride-hailing: Whether Uber's own Puerto Rico cities page names each municipality, as checked on a set date; it is a yes/no listing, not a measure of coverage or driver availability.
groups.Road network: The road map built from OpenStreetMap that the observatory uses to draw transit routes along streets and to plan routes: which roads it keeps, the road classes and planning speeds (not speed limits), and how the router and the route drawing follow roads.
groups.Routes: The transit route lines on the map and the details of each route (operator, number or name, type of vehicle, colour, scheduled trips per day, first and last weekday departure, and how the line was drawn), including volunteer-mapped routes, such as públicos, that have no timetable.
groups.Service coverage and planning: How many residents live within 400 m of a scheduled stop and how many live more than 800 m from one, the 2020 Census block data behind those counts, places where stops of different operators are within 250 m of each other, and the fixed distances the observatory uses.
groups.Stops, stations and terminals: Counts of stops, bus stations, rail stations and ferry terminals in each municipality, and a record for each transport point (name, kind, location, operator and, where the source gives them, routes served, weekday calls, wheelchair boarding and shelter), separating scheduled stops from timetables from stops that volunteers mapped in OpenStreetMap.
groups.Timetable replay: The weekday, Saturday and Sunday trip files, and the rules that show where each vehicle should be right now according to its published timetable, which is a schedule replay and not live tracking.
groups.Transit access of residents: How many residents of each municipality (2020 Census) live within 400 m of a scheduled stop, as a count and as a share, the share when expired timetables are left out, and counts near stops of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI, the Integrated Transport Authority) and of municipal systems.
groups.Transit methods and categories: The definitions and rules behind the municipal transit fields: the kinds of transit feature, the words current, expiring and expired for timetables, the 400 m walking rule, how residents near a stop are counted by census block, and which fields update nightly and which only when all the data are rebuilt.
groups.Route planner: How the route planner measures a route you draw: its length and running time, the residents and tourism places near it, how much of it overlaps existing routes or lies in flood or protected areas, the municipalities it crosses and its connections, with the sampling and distance rules behind these figures.
groups.Route analysis: The bus routes of the ATI and of the municipal systems of the metro area and the east, one row each, compared on their weekday timetables: trips and frequency, length and scheduled speed, the high-volume intersections they cross at peak hours (an estimate from OpenStreetMap and FHWA HPMS), connections and residents near their stops (route_compare.json, the Route analysis page of the Knowledge Area).

system.docs.summary: This area explains how the observatory counts, rescales and compares its numbers, from how places and jobs are counted to how maps are coloured, how the route planner measures a route and how to cite a figure. It helps you answer what a number counts, which year it covers, how sure it is and how it was calculated. Keep two things in mind: check the year or survey window, the snapshot and what is counted (for example jobs by workplace or people by home) before you compare two figures, and read ranks, colours and correlations as patterns, not as causes or as good and bad results.

groups.Build information: What the build file (meta.json) records: the snapshot name and date, the map box, the source credits, and the settings and facts of each build step (housing, land use, barrios, transit, time views) and of the place categories the build left out.
groups.Classes and colours: How a shaded map sorts municipalities into colour classes, why fixed classes keep colours comparable across years, how red and blue scales show distance from a centre value, how two datasets share one map, and how sized circles are drawn.
groups.Dollars and prices: How the 'Inflation-adjusted' option restates dollars of different years in the dollars of the latest year with a US price index, which is only an approximation for Puerto Rico.
groups.Ranking and comparing: How a municipality's rank is worked out, what the Housing page's middle value of the 78 municipalities means, and how the Ask the observatory chat finds the biggest rises and falls.
groups.Relationships between datasets: How the observatory measures whether two datasets move together across municipalities (correlation), how it finds the municipalities that sit far from the usual pattern, and how the chat ranks the strongest patterns; none of these shows cause.
groups.Rescaling a value: How the Analysis tab's 'Show as' menu rescales a dataset: per resident or per square kilometre, share of the island or of local jobs, comparison with Puerto Rico (index, difference, location quotient), change since a base year, and percentile.
groups.Snapshot counts: The counts the build records for one snapshot: Overture place records, tourism places, listings, merged duplicates, places of worship, flood polygons, protected-area records, municipalities and 2020 Census residents, plus the confidence cut-off used for tourism places.
groups.Survey tables: Which Census Bureau survey tables and cells sit behind the income, work, commuting, vehicle, internet, housing and household figures, and how reliable the housing and household survey figures are.
groups.Time and vintages: How the observatory chooses which year to show, what 'latest' means, how five-year survey windows are labelled, why the population series changes its base in 2020, how trend lines are drawn, and how snapshots are labelled and rebuilt.
groups.Uncertainty: What the margin of error means for survey figures, how it is calculated and shown, and where no margin is available.
groups.Using the observatory: How numbers are rounded and displayed, what a shared link stores about your view, and how to cite the observatory and its sources.
groups.Data inventory and wish list: The inventory file that lists every published data file with its size and its share of the hosting limit, and the wanted-data list of datasets that could be added, with their source, license as understood so far and status.
groups.Small-area estimates: How to read survey estimates for census tracts, block groups and barrios: margins of error, empty values, medians and rates, why barrios are read from the Census Bureau's own rows, and what the small-area reader downloads.
groups.Exposure series: How the exposure counts are made (blocks counted whole by their internal point), how they were checked, how a share is worked out, and what is not included yet.

system.tools.summary: This area describes the observatory's own tools (the 2D map and its tabs, the 3D + Time view, the Housing page, search, the Ask the observatory chat, links and downloads, and the lists of the observatory's data files), so you can see what each switch, menu and colour shows, how to save or share it, and where the data behind it are described. Read each legend, because the same colour means different numbers on different layers, and a darker colour means a higher value, not a better result. Several layers are planning aids, not live or exact data: vehicles replay timetables, flood and sea level layers show mapped zones or what-if heights, and the route planner is not an engineering study.

groups.2D map: Analysis tab: The Analysis tab, where datasets (mostly yearly) are shaded or sized on the map, and its workbench panel with table, scatter and trend views, including the year control, 'Show as' options, inflation adjustment and the dataset information window.
groups.2D map: Map layers tab: The switches, buttons and menus of the Map layers tab (tourism places and their filters, flood zones, sea level rise, transit, protected areas, land use, boundaries and barrios), what a click on the map opens, and how municipalities are shaded in five groups.
groups.2D map: Municipality and Rankings tabs: The profile of one municipality, the ranking of municipalities on one measure, and the download of the municipality table as a CSV (comma-separated values) file.
groups.2D map: Transit tab: The Transit tab's summary figures, the box that says which real-time data exist, the list of operators, the switches for scheduled vehicles, residents far from service and points where two transit systems meet, and the route planner.
groups.2D map: page and controls: The OpenStreetMap base map, side panel and top bar of the 2D map, the About tab, and the '?' help buttons.
groups.3D + Time view: The 3D view of Puerto Rico with its terrain, buildings, tourism places, municipality columns, hazard, transit, land use and protected-area layers, the three clocks (a day of transit, sea level by year and storm tracks since 1851), the route planner and how to move around.
groups.Ask the observatory (chat): The chat box that answers questions about the Analysis tab's datasets in English or Spanish using rules, not a language model, with the kinds of answer it gives, how it measures relationships between datasets, and what stays on your device.
groups.Data dictionary page: The data dictionary page, with its search, filters, citations and downloads, and the dictionary.json file it reads, which you can download.
groups.Data management page: The Data management page: every published data file with its records, fields, values, size, dates and compliance review, the growth of the published data and the counts of what is not published.
groups.Housing page: The Housing page, which reproduces key tables of Foundation for Puerto Rico's 2023 housing study as printed and adds live data for all 78 municipalities, with its year bar, maps and ranked charts, municipality profile, data catalog, affordability chart and 'Full data' window.
groups.Place names and search: The place-name index behind the search boxes, its name types and how it is built, how search matches what you type, and the search box itself.
groups.Search, links and downloads: The shareable links of the 2D map, the Analysis tab, the 3D view and the Housing page, the CSV and GeoJSON downloads, and the planned-route file.

groups.Change since 2008-2012: How much median household income and the share of adults with a bachelor's degree changed in each municipality between the 2008-2012 survey period and the latest one; the income change is in dollars not adjusted for price rises.
groups.Education: The share of adults 25 and over with a bachelor's degree or higher, from five-year Census Bureau surveys, as a series over time and as a single value for the latest survey period.
groups.Degrees awarded: How many degrees and certificates the colleges in each municipio awarded every academic year since 2014-15, by level and broad field (IPEDS).
groups.School conditions: Chronic absence, students per counselor, schools with a nurse and schools with no counselor in public schools, by municipio, from the Civil Rights Data Collection (2017-18 and 2021-22).
groups.Test results: The share of public school students proficient in reading (Spanish) and math on Puerto Rico's test (META-PR), by municipio, school years 2014-15 to 2018-19.

groups.Vehicles and internet: The share of households with no vehicle, with an internet subscription and with no internet access, from five-year Census Bureau surveys.
groups.Public safety: Type I crimes reported to the Police by municipality and year, from the Police's December reports: all eight crimes, violent crimes, property crimes and murders.

groups.Barrios: The outlines of the 901 barrios, the Census Bureau's districts inside municipalities, with each barrio's name, municipality, Census code and area.
groups.Boundary methods: How the boundaries were chosen and drawn: cut at the shoreline instead of out to sea, simplified for display, which barrios are used, and how barrio counts are worked out.
groups.Land area: Each municipality's land area in square kilometers from the 2020 Census, leaving out water, which is the base for per-area figures.
groups.Municipalities and regions: The municipality name that ties every statistic and place to a municipality, and the seven tourism regions of the Puerto Rico Tourism Company.
groups.Municipality boundaries: The outline of each of the 78 municipalities, with its names, Census code, land area, 2020 Census population and housing units, and tourism region.
groups.Geography crosswalk: The list of every area the observatory joins data to (the island, tourism regions, municipios, barrios, census tracts and block groups): each one's code, parent, names, land area, 2020 residents and housing units and an internal point, the weights that carry numbers from barrios to tracts, and the block table they are counted from.
groups.Census tracts and block groups: The simplified outlines of the 939 census tracts and 2,513 block groups that have land. They are for drawing only, never for area or distance.

health.summary: This area describes access to health care in Puerto Rico's 78 municipalities, from the public lists of HRSA, the Health Resources and Services Administration (an agency of the US Department of Health and Human Services): where community health centers that hold a federal grant (or look-alike status) have sites, and where HRSA has designated shortage areas of primary care, dental and mental health practitioners, with each area's priority score, the practitioners still needed and the share of need met. It does not yet cover hospitals, health outcomes or insurance. Keep two things in mind: the figures count what HRSA lists and measure it by HRSA's own federal formulas, so they are not a count of all the care in a place; and a municipality with no shortage value is not rated as a shortage area in HRSA's file, which is different from missing data.

groups.Health centers: Permanent sites and mobile vans of community health centers that hold a federal health center grant or look-alike status, counted for each municipality from HRSA's list of sites.
groups.Primary care shortage areas: HRSA's designations of areas whose low-income residents have too few primary care physicians: the priority score, the physicians still needed and the share of need met, for municipalities that have a designation.
groups.Dental shortage areas: HRSA's designations of areas whose low-income residents have too few dentists: the priority score, the dentists still needed and the share of need met, for municipalities that have a designation.
groups.Mental health shortage areas: HRSA's designations of areas whose low-income residents have too few mental health providers (in Puerto Rico, psychiatrists): the priority score, the providers still needed and the share of need met, for municipalities that have a designation.
groups.Health care providers: Health care providers registered with a practice address in each municipio, by type, from the NPPES registry: physicians, psychiatrists, dentists, nurse practitioners and physician assistants, other mental health providers and pharmacists.

infrastructure.energy.summary: This area describes how electricity is made and used in Puerto Rico. It holds EIA's inventory of power plants of 1 MW or more (each plant on the map with its capacity by technology, and the plants, capacity and renewable capacity of each municipio) and OpenStreetMap's transmission lines of 230, 115 and 38 kV. Keep two limits in mind: rooftop solar, which LUMA counted at 1,666 MW in September 2026, is not in EIA's inventory, so the renewable capacity here leaves most of Puerto Rico's solar out; and the 38 kV lines are about half mapped. Rooftop solar and batteries by municipio, reliability and cost are planned (HANDOFF decision 104).

groups.Power plants: EIA's monthly inventory of power plants of 1 MW or more (EIA-860M): each plant on the map, and the plants, capacity and renewable capacity of each municipality.
groups.Power grid: OpenStreetMap's high-voltage lines by voltage (230, 115 and 38 kV), simplified to about 100 m; substations counted, not drawn.
groups.Energy page: The figures of the Knowledge Area page Energy in Puerto Rico, from LUMA's filings with the Energy Bureau, EIA and FEMA.
groups.Energy by municipio: Batteries, electricity sales and smart meters by municipio from LUMA's filings, and the households paying $250 or more a month for electricity by municipio and barrio (ACS).

groups.Distance to essentials: How far residents live, along the roads, from a supermarket, any food store, a pharmacy, a bank or cooperativa, a library and a fire or EMS station, by barrio and municipio (estimates).
